courses.notes:
## Apprentice syllabus
What is industrial automation; open vs closed loop; P&ID reading; anatomy of a control loop; core terminology; final control element vs sensor vs controller

## Curated resources

### 🎬 VIDEO — Open loop vs closed loop
**Open Loop and Closed Loop Control Systems - Differences, Examples** — *Automation training channel*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DRrmHs7wKqs)

The concept every other module in this category rests on. Uses everyday examples before industrial ones, which is the right order for a fresher who has never seen a plant.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Reading a P&ID
**How to Read a P&ID? (Piping & Instrumentation Diagram)** — *RealPars*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j4EOTerfyTY)

Instrument bubbles, the line convention for field vs panel vs inaccessible, and ISA-5.1 letter codes. Our engineers cannot attend a kick-off meeting without this.

### 🎬 VIDEO — P&ID practice
**P&ID Diagram / Learn Instrumentation / Instrumentation and Control** — *Instrumentation training channel*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zPfJwWnwqLE)

Second pass on P&ID with different worked examples. Repetition on drawing-reading earns its slot - it is a skill, not a fact.

### 🚧 What is industrial automation — NEEDS REVIEW
R1 - NO ADEQUATE SOURCE. The RealPars Industrial Automation playlist (link for reference) contains suitable introductory material, but no single stable video URL could be confirmed. What is needed: one 8-15 minute video answering 'what is industrial automation and where does a DCS sit'. Strong candidate for internal content - it is also the natural place to introduce MICROSYS and Microverse.

courses.notes:
## Adept syllabus
PID basics; proportional/integral/derivative action; direct vs reverse action; auto/manual/bumpless transfer; the four standard loops - flow, level, pressure, temperature

## Curated resources

### 🎬 VIDEO — What a PID controller does
**PID Controller Explained** — *RealPars*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fv6dLTEvl74)

Starts from on/off control and builds to why P, I and D each exist. The thermostat analogy survives translation to any process. Reference explanation for this level.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Direct vs reverse controller action
**Direct and Reverse Acting Controllers** — *Process control lecture channel*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HMn2TSqgbaQ)

The most common configuration error our engineers make in the field. Explained against a liquid level example with valve action included, which is exactly how it bites on site.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Controller action - academic treatment
**Direct and reverse acting controller - control lecture** — *Memorial University (Process Dynamics and Control)*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b-0NxDmaWXM)

University course material on the same topic. Worth pairing because direct/reverse also depends on valve fail-action, and two independent explanations reduce the chance a wrong assumption sticks.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Analysing controller action in a strategy
**How to Analyze PID Controller Actions** — *InstrumentationTools*
[Open resource](https://instrumentationtools.com/analyze-controller-actions/)

Covers the subtlety the videos skip: a reverse-acting controller's output INCREASES when its setpoint increases. This trips people up constantly once remote setpoints and cascade appear at Master level.

courses.title: Industrial Automation Concepts & Process Control — Master
courses.description: Module 1 of 11 — Industrial Automation Concepts & Process Control. Control theory spine. Every other category assumes this.
courses.notes:
## Master syllabus
PID tuning methods (open-loop, Ziegler-Nichols, lambda); cascade; ratio; split-range; feedforward; override and selective control; deadtime compensation

## Curated resources

### 🎬 VIDEO — PID tuning - open-loop step method
**PID Tuning Using the Ziegler-Nichols Open-Loop Step Method** — *Control engineering channel*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nfOGY4GlEgI)

The reaction-curve method is the one usable on a running plant, unlike the closed-loop ultimate-gain method which requires driving the loop to oscillation. Verify the channel before assigning.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Tuning methods compared
**PID Tuning via Classical Methods** — *Engineering LibreTexts (Chemical Process Dynamics and Controls)*
[Open resource](https://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Industrial_and_Systems_Engineering/Chemical_Process_Dynamics_and_Controls_(Woolf)/09:_Proportional-Integral-Derivative_(PID)_Control/9.03:_PID_Tuning_via_Classical_Methods)

Open textbook covering Ziegler-Nichols closed and open loop plus Cohen-Coon, with the tuning tables and the deadtime condition that makes Cohen-Coon the right choice. Gives the engineer the formulas, not just the procedure.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Cascade control principle
**Introduction to Cascade Control** — *LearnChemE (University of Colorado Boulder)*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EPaQWBWp064)

Clean block-diagram derivation of why the inner loop must be faster than the outer one. Academic, short and precise - the correct grounding before applying it.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Cascade, override and split-range together
**Special Control Structures: Cascade, Override and Split Range Control** — *IDC Technologies technical reference*
[Open resource](https://www.idc-online.com/technical_references/pdfs/mechanical_engineering/Special_Control_Structures_Cascade_Override_and_Split_Range_Control.pdf)

All three structures in one document with the heat exchanger worked example, inner-loop stability condition, and the series vs parallel cascade distinction. Covers split-range and override which the videos do not.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Split-range control
**Split Range Control and Cascade Control** — *Chemical / process engineering course channel*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Is7-0GxovOs)

Split range appears constantly on our jobs - reactor jacket heating/cooling, dual fuel firing. Covers valve sequencing and the deadband problem at the changeover point.

courses.description: Module 1 of 11 — Industrial Automation Concepts & Process Control. Control theory spine. Every other category assumes this.
courses.notes:
## Legend syllabus
Advanced regulatory control; model-based and APC concepts; loop performance assessment; valve stiction and oscillation diagnosis; control strategy design from scratch

## Curated resources

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Tuning as an engineering discipline
**The Guide to PID Tuning** — *IPCOS (control consultancy)*
[Open resource](https://ureaknowhow.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/2020-IPCOS-PID-Tuning.pdf)

Consultancy guide comparing trial-and-error, Ziegler-Nichols, Cohen-Coon and model-based tuning, including why the Ziegler-Nichols 25% overshoot design criterion is wrong for most process loops. The step from applying a recipe to choosing a method.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Diagnosing loops that will not tune
**Getting the Best Performance from Challenging Control Loops** — *OptiControls*
[Open resource](https://www.opticontrols.com/files/documents/getting_best_performance.pdf)

The Legend skill: recognising that a loop is oscillating because of valve stiction, deadband or loop interaction rather than tuning. Includes the stick-slip signature (sawtooth OP, square PV) and the 0.5% manual step test to confirm it. No amount of retuning fixes a sticking valve.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Loop performance in a plant context
**Analyzing and Improving Control Loop Performance** — *Power Engineering*
[Open resource](https://www.power-eng.com/operations-maintenance/analyzing-and-improving-control-loop-performance/)

Applies the same diagnosis to power plant loops, including positioner overshoot and cyclical interaction between tightly coupled loops. Directly relevant to our captive power work, where feedwater and drum pressure loops fight each other routinely.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Model predictive and multivariable control
**Understanding Model Predictive Control (7-part series)** — *MathWorks*
[Open resource](https://www.mathworks.com/videos/series/understanding-model-predictive-control.html)

Series landing page - assign parts 1 to 3 for the concepts (prediction horizon, constraint handling, MIMO interaction) and skip the toolbox-specific parts unless the engineer will build a model. Handling loop interaction rather than tuning around it is what separates Legend from Master.

## Apprentice syllabus
Sensor types; 4-20 mA; RTD and thermocouple basics; signal types (AI/AO/DI/DO); tag numbering; two-wire vs four-wire

## Curated resources

### 🎬 VIDEO — The 4-20 mA signal
**4-20 mA Current Loop - History, Why, Advantages, Disadvantages** — *InstrumentationTools*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qyl_dvbgG2Y)

Why 4 mA and not 0 mA - live zero, broken wire detection, immunity to voltage drop. Every signal our IO cards read is this. Nothing else in this category makes sense without it.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Temperature sensing technologies
**Understanding Temperature Sensor Technology: RTDs, Thermocouples, and Thermistors** — *RealPars*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J2ulD-bPTS4)

Covers all three families in one pass so the apprentice can identify what is in front of them on site. Resistance vs Seebeck voltage explained without maths.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Choosing RTD or thermocouple
**RTD vs Thermocouple: Which is Better for Your Needs?** — *RealPars*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xeriqPQyhQ)

The selection question rather than the physics. The 800 degC crossover point and the accuracy-versus-range trade-off are the two facts an apprentice must retain.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Level by differential pressure
**DP Level Measurement Explained** — *RealPars*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ylhwPcyieTc)

Point vs continuous, direct vs indirect, and how hydrostatic head becomes a 4-20 mA signal. DP level is on almost every job we do, from sugar to water treatment.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Loop wiring in practice
**The Fundamentals of 4-20 mA Current Loops (recorded webinar)** — *Precision Digital*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0v9ZCD3oL1M)

Introductory class explicitly aimed at people who handle process signals but are not electrical engineers - which describes most of our projects team. Goes past the concept into actual loop wiring.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Control valve types
**What Are the Different Types of Control Valves?** — *Emerson / Fisher*
[Open resource](https://videos.emerson.com/detail/videos/fisher/video/6281259529001/what-are-the-different-types-of-control-valves)

OEM animation covering sliding stem vs rotary, motion type and pressure recovery. Hosted on Emerson's own video library rather than YouTube - check playback from site before assigning.

**When to Use an RTD vs. a Thermocouple Temperature Sensor** — *Ashcroft*
[Open resource](https://blog.ashcroft.com/rtd-vs-thermocouple-temperature-sensor)

Goes where the Apprentice videos stop: 2-, 3- and 4-wire RTD configurations and why 3-wire is the industrial default, plus the Type K/J/E/N comparison table. This is the detail that decides a termination drawing.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Loop budget and signal integrity
**4-20 mA Current Loop Basics: Wiring, EMC and Budgeting** — *PR Electronics*
[Open resource](https://www.prelectronics.com/the-fundamentals-of-4-20-ma-current-loops/)

Introduces the loop budget calculation - supply voltage against transmitter, receiver and cable resistance. First point where the engineer computes something rather than recognising it.

## Master syllabus
Loop wiring and loop drawings; loop budget and barrier calculation; calibration; hazardous area classification; IS barriers; hook-up drawings; control valve sizing

## Curated resources

### 🎬 VIDEO — Control valve sizing and selection
**Webinar: Control Valve Sizing and Selection (Fisher Technology Quick Talk)** — *Emerson / Fisher*
[Open resource](https://videos.emerson.com/detail/videos/control-valves/video/6160031388001/webinar:-control-valve-sizing-and-selection---fisher-technology-quick-talk)

Equipment parameters, flow media states, preliminary sizing calculation, selection, then re-running the calculation to confirm. That iterate-and-confirm loop is the Master-level habit, not the formula.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — The control valve reference
**Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition - chapters 1 to 5** — *Emerson*
[Open resource](https://www.emerson.com/en-us/automation/valves-actuators-regulators/control-valves/control-valve-handbook)

355 pages; assign chapters 1-5 only at this level - types, performance, actuators, accessories and sizing. The single most useful free document in this category. Archive a local PDF copy.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Hazardous area classification
**Hazardous Area Terminology** — *InstrumentationTools*
[Open resource](https://instrumentationtools.com/hazardous-area-terminology/)

Zones vs Divisions, gas groups, temperature classes and the Ex protection types. Note explicitly that IEC groups are NOT the same as NEC groups - our engineers meet both on export jobs and the mix-up is dangerous.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Loop calculation and barriers
**Basics of 4-20 mA Current Loop** — *InstrumentationTools*
[Open resource](https://instrumentationtools.com/basics-of-4-20ma-current-loop/)

The engineering treatment: 250 ohm receiver resistance, 2- vs 3-wire transmitters, where the loop is powered from the IO card versus a marshalling-cabinet barrier, and supply voltage selection.

courses.notes:
## Legend syllabus
Instrument selection for severe and corrosive service; cavitation and flashing; analyser and sampling systems; SIL-rated instruments and partial stroke testing; diagnostics via HART/FF

## Curated resources

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Severe service and valve failure modes
**Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition - severe service, steam conditioning and SIS chapters** — *Emerson*
[Open resource](https://www.emerson.com/en-us/automation/valves-actuators-regulators/control-valves/control-valve-handbook)

The later chapters: cavitation and flashing, desuperheaters, turbine bypass, and valves in safety instrumented systems. This is where an engineer learns why a correctly sized valve still destroys itself in eighteen months.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Intrinsic safety at design level
**Intrinsic Safety Protection Systems: Ex ia, Ex ib, Ex ic Explained** — *Automation Forum*
[Open resource](https://automationforum.co/intrinsic-safety-protection-systems-exia-exib-exic/)

Fault tolerance as the basis of the ia/ib/ic distinction, Zener barrier behaviour, and IEC 60079-11. Includes the judgement Legend level demands: Ex ic is never appropriate for a process safety function, however cost-effective it looks.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Non-contact level measurement
**Radar Level Measurement Explained** — *Endress+Hauser Learning Centre*
[Open resource](https://www.endress.com/en/support-overview/learning-center/radar-level-measurement-explained)

OEM technical explanation of time-of-flight versus FMCW, and when radar beats DP, hydrostatic, capacitive or ultrasonic. Relevant on tank farm, ethanol and water treatment jobs where the client specifies radar and we have to review the choice.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Positioner setup and valve diagnostics
**Setting Up and Calibrating Valve Positioners** — *Emerson Automation Experts*
[Open resource](https://www.emersonautomationexperts.com/2016/valves-actuators-regulators/setting-calibrating-valve-positioners/)

Practical zero, span and cam alignment procedure on a real positioner and actuator assembly. Pair with the stiction material in Category 1 Level 4 - a badly set positioner and a sticking valve look identical from the control room.

### 🚧 Analyser and sampling system design — NEEDS REVIEW
R1 - NO ADEQUATE SOURCE. Nothing free and authoritative was found covering sample conditioning system design, lag time calculation, or analyser house layout. This matters on our chemical, ethanol and ferro alloy jobs where the analyser is the loop. Options: ISA-76 series, or vendor training from the analyser supplier on the next job that includes one - make it a contract condition.

### 🚧 SIL-rated instruments and partial stroke testing — NEEDS REVIEW
R4 - PURCHASE / CERTIFICATION. Overlaps Category 8 Level 4, which has the same gap. Covers selecting certified transmitters and valves against a target SIL, and partial stroke test configuration on ESD valves. Same recommendation: buy IEC 61511-1:2016 and get an engineer certified before we take scope in this area.

CPU, IO modules, power supply, backplane; rack and node layout; IO module types and channel counts; hot-swap concepts

## Curated resources

### 🎬 VIDEO — What a control panel is
**Industrial Control Panel Basics** — *RSP Supply*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lNtmo5dK54o)

Starts with why panels exist at all, then the basic layout convention - where power comes in, where control lives, why things sit where they sit. Vendor-neutral on the layout principles. The right first ten minutes for a fresher who has never opened a cabinet door.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Panel components identified
**Introduction to Electrical Control Panels including PLCs and HMIs** — *Technician training channel*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NjXWcDPwHis)

Names every major component on sight - breakers, contactors, relays, terminal blocks, power supplies, DIN rail. Apprentices cannot follow a site conversation until they can name what they are looking at.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Reading a panel wiring diagram
**Wiring Diagrams Explained: Industrial Control Panel Basics** — *Automation training channel*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-oFO73uRv8o)

Navigating the pages of a panel drawing set - how sheets cross-reference, how wire numbers carry across. Pairs directly with the loop diagram material in Category 7 Apprentice; assign them in the same week.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Schematics for controls engineers
**Introduction to Electrical Wiring and Schematics for Controls and Automation Engineering** — *Controls engineering channel*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V-IwuBEa0PE)

Second pass on schematic conventions aimed specifically at controls rather than general electrical work. Repetition earns its slot here for the same reason it does on P&IDs - drawing-reading is a skill, not a fact.

## Adept syllabus
System sizing from an IO list; IO allocation and spare philosophy; marshalling vs direct termination; panel GA; wiring, ferruling, earthing and shielding

## Curated resources

### 🎬 VIDEO — Laying out a panel properly
**Tips on Laying Out Your Industrial Control Panel** — *Technician training channel*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SuOOrvxqQ48)

Component placement, wire duct sizing, separation of power from signal, and leaving room for the modifications that always come later. This is the module that most directly improves what leaves our own production floor.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Panel design and build end to end
**How to Design and Build an Industrial Control Panel** — *AutomationDirect*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lFfHbMDZgx8)

Chaptered walkthrough from enclosure selection through to a finished build. RETAINED UNDER HARD FILTER 8 as enclosure and build practice, not control product content - assign the panel construction chapters and skip the product catalogue sections.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Junction box, marshalling panel, system cabinet
**Marshalling Panel vs Junction Box vs System Cabinet: What Are the Differences?** — *Viox*
[Open resource](https://viox.com/marshalling-panel-vs-junction-box-vs-system-cabinet/)

Three enclosures our engineers name interchangeably and should not. Covers the IP rating ranges that apply to each and the physical size implications, which is where panel GA drawings start going wrong.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — What marshalling actually does
**What is a Marshalling Cabinet or Marshalling Panel?** — *Automation Forum*
[Open resource](https://automationforum.co/what-is-marshalling-cabinet-or-marshalling-panel/)

Names the three marshalling methods - cross-wire, fan-out and half-knit - which most of our engineers have used without knowing there is a choice being made. Explains why field multi-pair cable is broken out before it meets an IO card.

courses.title: Control System Hardware, Panel & Architecture Design — Master
courses.description: Module 3 of 11 — Control System Hardware, Panel & Architecture Design. Curated - see Cat03 sheet. The MICROSYS core.
courses.category: Control System Hardware, Panel & Architecture Design
courses.notes:
## Master syllabus
Redundancy schemes (CPU, power, communication, IO); UPS and battery sizing; panel heat load and cooling; remote IO architecture; distributed node design

## Curated resources

### 🎬 VIDEO — Panel design decisions
**The RIGHT Way to Design an Electrical Control Panel** — *Controls specialist training channel*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PGgPwdO8cxQ)

Design-level rather than build-level: the sequence of decisions and the ones that are expensive to reverse. Recent upload, so the practice reflected is current. Verify the channel before assigning.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Shield grounding, demonstrated
**Cable Noise: The Effect of Grounding the Shield Conductor** — *Instrumentation demonstration*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DOoyrsi6ctk)

A real bench test - signal cable placed beside a powered extension lead, grounded shield versus ungrounded, with the noise visible on the trace. Ten years old and still the clearest proof of the principle available. Watching it lands harder than reading it.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Instrument earthing principles
**Instrumentation Earthing: Types and Principle** — *InstrumentationTools*
[Open resource](https://instrumentationtools.com/instrumentation-earthing/)

States the rule that governs everything else: the screen is grounded at ONE source only, normally the cabinet, with the field end left floating and insulated. Grounding both ends creates a ground-loop current that becomes noise on the signal conductor itself. Also covers earth bar hierarchy through to the earth pit.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Choosing and terminating shields
**Cable Shielding: Purpose, Selection, Grounding** — *InstrumentationTools*
[Open resource](https://instrumentationtools.com/cable-shielding-purpose-selection-grounding/)

Screen construction types and what each is good for, plus the honest observation that most signal noise, spike and interference complaints trace back to poor grounding rather than to the instrument or the control system. Worth knowing before we accept blame on a commissioning call.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Marshalling cabinet design in practice
**Marshalling Cabinet Explained: Design, Wiring, FAT, SAT and Best Practices** — *Automation Forum*
[Open resource](https://automationforum.co/what-is-marshalling-cabinet/)

Design-level treatment including the constraints that bite on real jobs - IP54 minimum for indoor industrial, cooling needs once component heat accumulates, EMI and RFI emission affecting neighbouring equipment, and voltage transients from poor design damaging sensitive parts.

courses.title: Control System Hardware, Panel & Architecture Design — Legend
courses.description: Module 3 of 11 — Control System Hardware, Panel & Architecture Design. Curated - see Cat03 sheet. The MICROSYS core.
courses.category: Control System Hardware, Panel & Architecture Design
courses.notes:
## Legend syllabus
Full architecture design for large plants; multi-node and multi-building topologies; availability and MTBF estimation; migration and retrofit design on live plants

## Curated resources

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Grounding and bonding as a system
**Grounding and Bonding in Instrumentation and Control Systems** — *Automation Forum*
[Open resource](https://automationforum.co/grounding-and-bonding-in-instrumentation-control-systems/)

The Legend-level framing: bond all metal together, reference the signal ground ONCE, and ensure noise has only one path to earth. Includes the diagnostic signature - transmitter output unstable while the process is steady, noise increasing when a motor starts - that identifies a grounding fault rather than an instrument fault.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — When both ends is the right answer
**Proper Instrument Shield Grounding: Single versus Dual End Practices** — *Industrial Monitor Direct*
[Open resource](https://industrialmonitordirect.com/blogs/knowledgebase/instrument-cable-shield-grounding-single-vs-dual-end-practices)

Where Master learns the rule, Legend learns its limits. Single-end grounding is correct for low-frequency analogue signals, but for higher-frequency communication lines - Ethernet, Profibus, RS-485 - grounding at both ends can be correct. Knowing which case you are in is the distinction.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Redundancy architecture
**Communication and Power Redundancy for Control Devices** — *Control.com technical article*
[Open resource](https://control.com/technical-articles/communication-and-power-redundancy-for-control-devices/)

Master and reserve CPU behaviour, online versus standby modes, and redundant 24 V DC supplies to control hardware. Uses a hydropower plant control system as its worked example - directly relevant to our captive power work. Product references are incidental to the architecture content.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Sizing the UPS
**UPS Selection Factors for a Control System** — *InstrumentationTools*
[Open resource](https://instrumentationtools.com/ups-selection/)

The method rather than the formula: identify loads by location and by required backup duration, sum loads sharing the same battery backup, then draw the load distribution schematic. Control room at 30 minutes and substation at 2 hours are different UPS decisions, and treating them as one is how sizing goes wrong.

### 🚧 MICROSYS sizing and architecture design — NEEDS REVIEW
R5 - INTERNAL BY NATURE. The core of this category and the one thing no external source can ever provide: sizing a MICROSYS system from an IO list, rack and node layout rules, our spare IO philosophy, which redundancy options we offer at which price point, and multi-node topology limits. Everything above teaches the general principles; this teaches our system. Author it as a design manual - it doubles as the engineering reference our own team currently lacks.

### 🚧 Panel heat load and cooling calculation — NEEDS REVIEW
R1 - NO ADEQUATE SOURCE. Nothing free and rigorous was found for enclosure heat load calculation and cooling sizing. Everything available is an enclosure vendor's selection tool that returns an answer without showing the method - useless for teaching and useless when a client challenges the number. Fix: work from IEC 60890 (the calculation method for enclosure temperature rise, a paid standard) and write the module against our own standard panel builds, with our real component dissipation figures.

courses.notes:
## Apprentice syllabus
Serial vs Ethernet; master/slave and client/server; what a protocol is; RS-232/422/485; IP addressing, subnet mask, gateway; OSI model orientation

## Curated resources

### 🎬 VIDEO — Serial communication & physical layer
**What is RS485 and How it's used in Industrial Control Systems?** — *RealPars*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3wgKcUDlHuM)

Cleanest explanation of why RS-485 exists - multidrop, distance, noise immunity. Vendor-neutral. This is the physical layer under Modbus RTU and Profibus, so it comes first.

### 🚧 RS-485 reinforcement lesson — NEEDS REVIEW
R2 - CREATOR UNVERIFIABLE. Content looks appropriate and sits inside a structured series, but the channel and its back-catalogue could not be confirmed against the Part B creator classes. Verify before assigning, or drop the slot - Apprentice already has adequate RS-485 coverage.

### 🎬 VIDEO — Ethernet, IP addressing and OSI
**Network Fundamentals Explained: OSI Model, Subnetting, and More** — *UniFi / David Barger*
[Open resource](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lF9OFRz_suk)

IT-side content, but no engineer can configure a Profinet or Modbus TCP network without subnet masks and the OSI layers. No industrial channel covers this as clearly.

### 🎬 VIDEO — First protocol - what Modbus is

[Open resource](https://www.symestic.com/en-us/what-is/industrial-data-historian)

Draws the boundaries our engineers blur in client meetings: SCADA visualises and stores limited history, MES handles orders and OEE, a data lake is generic storage, and the historian is the raw source feeding all three. **What is Unified Namespace? A Real-World Guide** — *TT PSC*
[Open resource](https://ttpsc.com/en/blog/what-is-unified-namespace/)

Explains the shift from the linear sensor-PLC-SCADA-MES-ERP chain to hub-and-spoke, and insists on brownfield-first: build the UNS alongside existing systems rather than ripping anything out. ### 🚧 Historian configuration in practice — NEEDS REVIEW
R5 - INTERNAL BY NATURE. Tag selection, per-tag deadband tuning, retention policy, archive sizing and role-based access are configured differently in every product, and every available tutorial is for a competing historian. Author on Miralys. Pairs with the Category 6 Adept modules - build all three together as one internal content block.

The design-level treatment: every inter-zone flow documented as a conduit with source, destination, protocol, port, direction and controls, and the SL-1 to SL-4 security levels that determine the countermeasures. **NIST SP 800-82 Revision 3: Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security** — *NIST*
[Open resource](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2023/09/guide-operational-technology-ot-security-nist-publishes-sp-800-82-revision)

Free, authoritative and comprehensive - unusual in this field. Provides the OT overlay for the SP 800-53 control catalogue with tailored baselines for low, moderate and high-impact OT systems. This is the document to cite when a client asks what framework we work to.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Applying 800-82 without breaking the plant
**NIST SP 800-82 Explained: 12 Questions and Answers About OT Security** — *Security Scientist*
[Open resource](https://www.securityscientist.net/blog/12-questions-and-answers-about-nist-sp-800-82/)

Makes the point that separates OT security from IT security, and it is the Legend-level judgement in this category: if a security control or a bad patch causes a false SIS trip, you have created a safety incident. Every control must be assessed for its effect on uptime and safety, not only its security benefit.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — Where the standard itself is ambiguous
**Security Aspects of Zones and Conduits in IEC 62443** — *MDPI (peer-reviewed, Journal of Cybersecurity and Privacy)*
[Open resource](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-800X/6/2/52)

Peer-reviewed analysis showing IEC 62443 does not hold to a single definition of 'zone' across its parts, and that 62443-2-1 requires segmentation into zones without clearly distinguishing them from conduits. Knowing where a standard is genuinely unclear - rather than assuming you misread it - is a Legend trait.

### 📄 DOCUMENT — UNS implementation roadmap
**The Architect's Guide to Unified Namespace: Implementation Roadmap** — *Proxus*
[Open resource](https://proxus.io/blog/unified-namespace-architecture-guide/)

Five-phase rollout, edge gateway bridging and namespace design worked through with a concrete example. Cites IEC 62443-2-1, ISA-95/IEC 62264 and NIST SP 800-82r3 as its references, which is the correct posture: a UNS design that ignores the segmentation standard is a data project that will fail security review.

### 🚧 Miralys and Aletix plant-to-cloud architecture — NEEDS REVIEW
R5 - INTERNAL BY NATURE. How a MICROSYS system publishes to Miralys, where the edge gateway sits relative to the DMZ, what the conduit rules are, and how secure remote access is designed for our AMC work. This is our reference architecture and it should be a documented product artefact, not tribal knowledge held by two people. Writing it also gives us something to submit when a client's IT department reviews our proposal.

### 🚧 IEC 62443 certification path — NEEDS REVIEW
R4 - PURCHASE / CERTIFICATION. Free commentary takes us to competent, not credentialed. If we intend to make OT security a paid scope line rather than an assumed one, we need current copies of IEC 62443-2-1, -3-2 and -3-3, and at least one engineer with ISA/IEC 62443 certification. Add to the office library budget alongside the Category 6, 7 and 8 purchases.

**Surviving a Control System Migration Project** — *Plant Engineering*
[Open resource](https://www.plantengineering.com/surviving-a-control-system-migration-project/)

questions.question: What distinguishes a closed loop control system from an open loop one?

options.B: It measures the result and corrects for the difference
options.C: It uses electrical rather than pneumatic signals
options.D: It has more than one final control element
options.E: It cannot be put in manual

questions.rationale: Feedback. A closed loop measures the outcome and acts on the error; an open loop simply applies an output and hopes.

questions.question: A domestic toaster with a fixed timer is an example of:

options.B: Open loop control

questions.rationale: No measurement of how brown the toast actually is. Nothing is fed back, so nothing is corrected.

questions.question: In a control loop, the process variable (PV) is:

options.B: The measured value of the thing being controlled
options.E: The difference between setpoint and measurement

questions.rationale: The PV is what the transmitter reports. The setpoint is what you want it to be.

questions.question: In a control loop, the error is defined as:

options.B: Controller output minus valve position
options.D: The difference between two redundant transmitters

questions.rationale: Error is SP minus PV. Everything the controller does is a response to that number.

questions.question: Which of these is the final control element in a typical flow loop?

options.B: The differential pressure transmitter

questions.rationale: The final control element is what physically acts on the process, normally a control valve or a variable speed drive.

questions.question: Which of these is the sensing element in a typical temperature loop?

options.B: The RTD or thermocouple

questions.rationale: The RTD or thermocouple senses; the transmitter converts that into a signal the controller can read.

questions.question: The controller output is often abbreviated as:

options.B: SP

questions.rationale: OP or CO, the controller output. It is the signal sent to the final control element, expressed as a percentage.

questions.question: A controller placed in manual mode:

options.B: Holds its output where the operator sets it, ignoring the error

questions.rationale: In manual the operator sets the output directly. The measurement is still displayed but the controller no longer acts on the error.

questions.question: What does bumpless transfer mean?

options.A: The valve moves smoothly at all times
options.B: Switching between manual and automatic does not cause a step change in output
options.D: The loop cannot be switched to manual

questions.rationale: Switching modes does not jump the output. Without it, every mode change disturbs the process.

questions.question: Negative feedback in a control loop means:

options.B: The correction opposes the deviation
options.C: The error is subtracted from the controller output

questions.rationale: The loop acts to reduce the deviation. Positive feedback would drive it away and the loop would run away.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT part of a basic feedback loop?

options.B: Controller

questions.rationale: The historian records data but plays no part in closing the loop.

questions.question: A cascade of pumps started by a hardwired timer with no measurement of pressure is:

options.B: Open loop

questions.rationale: No pressure measurement is fed back, so nothing corrects for a wrong result.

questions.question: The purpose of a transmitter in a loop is to:

options.B: Convert the sensed physical quantity into a standard signal

questions.rationale: It converts a physical measurement into a standard signal, typically 4-20 mA, that the control system can read.

questions.question: A disturbance in control terms is:

options.B: Any influence on the process that the controller did not command

questions.rationale: A disturbance is an uncommanded influence, such as a change in feed temperature or ambient conditions, that the loop must reject.

questions.question: Why is automatic control preferred over manual operation for most plant loops?

options.A: It removes the need for operators
options.B: It responds continuously and consistently, at a speed and consistency a human cannot sustain
options.D: It eliminates the need for instruments
options.E: It removes the need for alarms

questions.rationale: Consistency and speed. A human can control a loop for ten minutes; a controller does it for ten years without getting distracted.

questions.question: In the phrase 'the loop is in auto', auto means:

options.B: The controller is acting on the error to drive the PV to setpoint

questions.rationale: Auto means the controller is computing its own output from the error. It says nothing about where the setpoint comes from.

questions.question: A loop whose setpoint comes from another controller rather than from the operator is said to be in:

options.B: Auto

questions.rationale: Cascade, or remote setpoint. The operator sets the outer loop; the outer loop sets this one.

questions.question: Which statement about the controller's job is correct?

options.B: It decides how far to move the final control element based on the error
options.C: It converts pneumatic signals to electric

questions.rationale: The controller's only job is deciding the output from the error. Everything else in the loop is measurement or actuation.

questions.question: On a P&ID, a plain circle containing a tag represents an instrument that is:

options.B: Mounted on the front of a main panel

questions.rationale: A plain circle is field mounted. A horizontal line through it means panel mounted; a dashed line means inaccessible or rear of panel.

questions.question: In ISA-5.1 tag FIC-101, what does the first letter F indicate?

options.B: The measured variable is flow

questions.rationale: The first letter is the measured or initiating variable. F is flow, T temperature, P pressure, L level.

questions.question: In tag FIC-101, what do the succeeding letters I and C indicate?

options.B: Indicate and Control

questions.rationale: Succeeding letters give the functions performed: I for indicate, C for control, T for transmit, R for record, A for alarm.

questions.question: What does the tag LAHH-205 describe?

options.A: A level alarm at a high setting
options.B: A level alarm, high high

questions.rationale: L level, A alarm, HH high high. The doubled letter denotes the second, more severe trip point.

questions.question: What does PSV stand for on a P&ID?

options.B: Pressure Safety Valve

questions.rationale: Pressure safety valve, a mechanical relief device. Do not confuse it with a controlled pressure valve, PV or PCV.

questions.question: A dashed line between an instrument bubble and the process typically represents:

options.B: An electrical signal

questions.rationale: In ISA-5.1 a dashed line is an electrical signal. A line with double crosshatches is pneumatic.

questions.question: On a P&ID, a solid heavy line represents:

options.B: A software or data link

questions.rationale: Heavy solid lines are the process itself. Signal lines are drawn lighter and coded by type.

questions.question: A square with a circle inside, containing a tag, generally indicates:

options.B: A shared display or shared control function, such as a DCS point

questions.rationale: The square-with-circle is the shared display, shared control symbol - a DCS or PLC-based function rather than a discrete instrument.

questions.question: In a tag such as TT-301, the number 301 usually indicates:

options.B: The loop number, often grouped by plant unit or area

questions.rationale: The loop number, conventionally grouped by area - 1xx for unit 1, 3xx for unit 3, and so on.

questions.question: Two instruments tagged TT-301 and TIC-301 tell you that:

options.B: They belong to the same control loop, one transmitting and one controlling

questions.rationale: Same loop number means same loop. The transmitter measures and the controller acts, both on loop 301.

questions.question: What does FV normally denote?

options.A: Flow Valve, the control valve in a flow loop
options.B: Field Verified

questions.rationale: FV is the final control element in a flow loop. FCV is also used; project conventions vary and the legend sheet governs.

questions.question: The letter A as a succeeding letter in an instrument tag means:

options.B: Alarm

questions.rationale: As a succeeding letter, A means alarm. As a first letter, A means analysis.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the legend or symbol sheet issued with a P&ID set?

options.B: To define the symbols, line types and abbreviations used on that specific project
options.C: To give the pipe stress calculations

questions.rationale: Projects deviate from ISA-5.1 and document those deviations on the legend sheet. Read it before reading the drawings.

questions.question: An instrument bubble drawn with a solid horizontal line through the middle indicates the device is:

options.B: Mounted on the front of a main panel accessible to the operator

questions.rationale: A single solid line means front of main panel. A dashed line means the operator cannot reach it.

questions.question: What does the letter Y as a succeeding letter usually indicate?

options.B: A relay, compute or convert function

questions.rationale: Y denotes a relay, computing or converting function, such as a signal selector or square root extractor.

questions.question: A control valve on a P&ID is annotated FC. This means:

options.B: Fail Closed on loss of air or signal

questions.rationale: FC on a valve is its fail action - closed on loss of motive power. FO is fail open, FL is fail last.

questions.question: Why does the fail action of a valve matter to a control engineer?

options.B: It determines the required controller action and the plant's safe state on power or air failure

questions.rationale: Fail action decides the plant's safe state and, together with the process, decides whether the controller must be direct or reverse acting.

questions.question: On a P&ID you see LT-201, LIC-201 and LV-201. What have you found?

options.B: A complete level control loop - measurement, control and final element

questions.rationale: Transmitter, controller and valve on the same loop number is a complete loop.

questions.question: A P&ID shows a transmitter connected to a controller, and the controller connected to two valves. This suggests:

options.B: A split-range or duplex arrangement

questions.rationale: One output driving two valves is the signature of split range - each valve takes a portion of the controller output range.

questions.question: On a P&ID, an instrument bubble with a hexagonal outline commonly denotes:

options.B: A computer or software function

questions.rationale: The hexagon is the computer function symbol in ISA-5.1, used for calculated or software-only functions.

questions.question: You are asked to produce an IO list from a P&ID. Which instruments appear on it?

options.B: Only those that are physically wired to the control system

questions.rationale: The IO list contains only what connects to the control system. Local gauges and mechanical relief devices appear on the instrument index but not on the IO list.

questions.question: A line on a P&ID drawn with small circles along it typically indicates:

options.B: A data link or software connection

questions.rationale: Small circles denote an internal system or software link between functions in the same control system.

questions.question: The tag PDT-402 indicates a transmitter measuring:

options.B: Pressure at a distance

questions.rationale: P for pressure, D as a modifier for differential, T for transmit. Modifier letters change the meaning of the first letter.

questions.question: On a P&ID, HS-110 most likely represents:

options.B: A hand switch

questions.rationale: H is hand, S is switch. Hand switches are operator-initiated devices such as a local start/stop.

questions.question: A P&ID is issued 'For Construction'. What does that mean for you?

options.A: It is a concept only and will change substantially
options.B: It is approved for the plant to be built to, and changes now require formal change control

questions.rationale: For Construction means the drawing is approved to build from. Later changes require change control, and that is where cost and schedule impact appear.

questions.question: Why must the control engineer read the P&ID rather than working only from the IO list?

options.A: The IO list has no tag numbers
options.B: The P&ID shows the process relationships, fail actions and loop intent that a flat list cannot
options.E: The IO list is not a contractual document

questions.rationale: The IO list tells you what points exist. Only the P&ID tells you what they are for and how they relate to each other.

questions.question: Two P&IDs of adjacent units show the same line leaving one and entering the other. The marker used at that boundary is called:

options.B: An off-page or continuation reference

questions.rationale: A continuation or off-page reference, giving the drawing number the line continues on. Following these is how you trace a system across a drawing set.

questions.question: In a PID controller, the proportional term produces an output that is proportional to:

options.A: The rate of change of the error
options.B: The accumulated error over time

questions.rationale: P acts on the error now. I acts on its history, D on its trend.

questions.question: What is the characteristic weakness of proportional-only control?

options.B: It leaves a steady-state offset from setpoint
options.C: It is too slow to respond
options.E: It cannot be used in auto

questions.rationale: P-only needs a non-zero error to produce a non-zero output change, so it settles away from setpoint. Integral action is what removes that offset.

questions.question: The integral term of a PID controller acts on:

options.B: The accumulated error over time

questions.rationale: It sums error over time and keeps driving the output until the error is zero, which is exactly what eliminates offset.

questions.question: The derivative term responds to:

options.B: The rate of change of the error or PV

questions.rationale: D responds to the trend, giving the controller a degree of anticipation on slow processes.

questions.question: Why is derivative action normally avoided on flow control loops?

options.B: Flow measurement is noisy and derivative amplifies noise
options.C: Flow valves cannot respond fast enough

questions.rationale: Flow signals are inherently noisy and D differentiates that noise straight onto the valve, producing constant small movements and wear.

questions.question: Proportional band is related to controller gain by:

options.B: PB = 100 / Kc

questions.rationale: PB percent equals 100 divided by gain. A gain of 5 is a proportional band of 20 percent.

questions.question: A controller has a gain of 2.5. What is its proportional band, in percent? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: 100 divided by 2.5 equals 40 percent. Knowing both conventions matters because vendors and older equipment disagree on which they display.

questions.question: A controller displays a proportional band of 200 percent. What is the equivalent gain? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: 100 divided by 200 equals 0.5. A wide proportional band is a low gain - a detuned, sluggish loop.

questions.question: Increasing controller gain generally makes a loop:

options.B: Faster to respond but closer to instability

questions.rationale: Higher gain means a bigger output for the same error - faster correction but less stability margin. This trade-off is the whole of tuning.

questions.question: Reducing integral time (in minutes per repeat) has what effect?

options.B: Strengthens integral action
options.C: Has no effect on integral action

questions.rationale: Less time per repeat means the integral repeats the proportional action more often, so the action is stronger. Note that some vendors use reset rate in repeats per minute, where the relationship inverts.

questions.question: What is integral windup?

options.A: The integral term resetting to zero on mode change
options.B: The integral term continuing to accumulate while the output is saturated
options.C: Derivative kick on a setpoint change
options.D: Oscillation caused by too much gain
options.E: The valve winding to its stop

questions.rationale: When the output is already at a limit the integral keeps accumulating, so recovery is delayed while it unwinds. Anti-windup logic exists to prevent this.

questions.question: Derivative kick refers to:

options.B: A large output spike when the setpoint is stepped, caused by derivative acting on the error

questions.rationale: If derivative acts on error, a setpoint step produces a near-infinite rate of change. Acting on PV instead of error avoids it, which is why most modern controllers do exactly that.

questions.question: Select all statements that are true of a flow control loop.

options.B: It typically uses high controller gain

questions.rationale: Flow is fast and noisy, so it wants low gain with strong integral and no derivative. High gain on a noisy fast loop produces valve chatter.

questions.question: Select all statements that are true of a temperature control loop on a heat exchanger.

options.B: It often has significant dead time
options.D: It usually needs very strong integral action
options.E: The measurement is usually quieter than a flow measurement

questions.rationale: Temperature is slow, dead-time prone and relatively quiet, which is where derivative earns its place. Strong integral on a slow loop causes overshoot.

questions.question: Why is a level loop on a surge vessel often tuned loosely, or run with P-only?

options.B: The vessel is there to absorb variation, so tight level control defeats its purpose
options.C: Integral action is unavailable on level loops
options.D: Level is too fast to control
options.E: The valve cannot move slowly enough

questions.rationale: A surge vessel exists to smooth flow. Controlling its level tightly passes every inlet disturbance straight downstream, which is the opposite of what the vessel is for.

questions.question: A level process is described as integrating. That means:

options.B: With a constant imbalance between inflow and outflow the level keeps changing and does not settle
options.C: The controller must use integral action
options.D: The level sensor sums over time

questions.rationale: An integrating process does not self-regulate. Any imbalance drives the level continuously, which is why level loops behave differently from flow or temperature.

questions.question: A direct-acting controller does what when the process variable rises above setpoint?

options.B: Increases its output

questions.rationale: Direct acting means PV up, output up.

questions.question: A reverse-acting controller does what when the process variable rises above setpoint?

options.B: Decreases its output

questions.rationale: Reverse acting means PV up, output down. This is the more common case in process control.

questions.question: A tank level is controlled by throttling the outlet valve, which is air-to-open. As level rises, the valve must:

options.B: Open

questions.rationale: Rising level needs more outflow, so the valve opens. With air-to-open that means increasing output, so the controller is direct acting.

questions.question: A tank level is controlled by throttling the INLET valve, which is air-to-open. As level rises, the controller must be:

options.B: Reverse acting

questions.rationale: Rising level needs less inflow, so the valve must close, so output must fall. Reverse acting. Same measured variable as the previous question, opposite answer - which is why this catches people out.

questions.question: A steam heater controls outlet temperature with an air-to-open steam valve. The controller action should be:

options.B: Reverse

questions.rationale: Temperature too high means less steam, so the valve closes, so output falls. Reverse acting.

questions.question: The same steam heater is refitted with an air-to-CLOSE steam valve. The controller action must now be:

options.B: Direct

questions.rationale: Reversing the valve action reverses the required controller action. The loop must remain net negative feedback, so if one element flips, another must.

questions.question: The rule that governs controller action selection is:

options.A: Always use reverse acting for safety
options.B: The total loop must be negative feedback, counting the process, the valve action and the controller
options.C: Match the action to the transmitter type
options.D: Direct for analogue, reverse for digital
options.E: Match the action to the fail position only

questions.rationale: Count the sign changes around the whole loop. The product must be negative feedback, or the loop runs away.

questions.question: A loop is commissioned and the PV runs hard away from setpoint to the limit as soon as it is put in auto. The first thing to suspect is:

options.B: Controller action set the wrong way round

questions.rationale: Running to a limit immediately on auto is the classic signature of positive feedback from wrong controller action. It fails the same way every time and takes seconds to test.

questions.question: An air-to-open control valve is also described as:

options.B: Fail closed

questions.rationale: Air to open means loss of air closes it, so it is fail closed. Vendors use both terms and they mean the same thing.

questions.question: Why is the fail position of a valve chosen on process safety grounds rather than control convenience?

options.B: On loss of air or power the plant must move to its safe state
options.E: It is a regulatory tag requirement

questions.rationale: Fail position defines the safe state. The control engineer then adapts the controller action to whatever the process safety decision requires - never the other way round.

questions.question: Select all things that must be known before deciding a controller's action.

options.A: Whether the measured variable rises or falls when the valve opens
options.B: The valve's air-to-open or air-to-close action
options.E: Whether a positioner reverses the signal

questions.rationale: Process direction, valve action and any reversal in the positioner. Range and gain affect tuning, not action.

questions.question: A pressure control loop vents gas through an air-to-open valve to atmosphere. The controller should be:

options.B: Reverse acting

questions.rationale: Pressure too high means vent more, so the valve opens, so output rises. Direct acting.

questions.question: A positioner is configured with reverse action while the valve is air-to-open. The net effect at the valve is:

options.B: Air to close

questions.rationale: A reversing positioner flips the effective action. This is a real trap because the valve nameplate still says air-to-open.

questions.question: On a cooling loop, chilled water flows through an air-to-open valve to control jacket temperature. The controller action is:

options.B: Reverse acting

questions.rationale: Temperature too high means more cooling, so the valve opens, so output rises. Direct acting - the opposite of the same loop heated by steam.

questions.question: Which document should tell you a valve's fail action before you configure the controller?

options.B: The P&ID and the valve datasheet

questions.rationale: The P&ID carries the FC/FO annotation and the datasheet confirms it. Configuring action from memory is how loops get commissioned backwards.

questions.question: In block diagram terms, process gain is:

options.A: The change in PV divided by the change in controller output at steady state
options.B: The controller's proportional setting
options.C: The valve travel per unit signal
options.E: The rate of change of the PV

questions.rationale: Process gain is delta PV over delta OP at steady state. It is a property of the process and equipment, not of the controller.

questions.question: A process with a negative process gain means:

options.B: Increasing the controller output causes the PV to fall

questions.rationale: Negative process gain simply means the PV moves opposite to the output, as in a cooling loop. The controller action must account for its sign.

questions.question: Dead time in a process is:

options.A: The time the controller spends in manual
options.B: The delay between an output change and any observable response in the PV
options.C: The time constant of the process
options.D: The scan period of the controller

questions.rationale: Pure delay before anything happens. It is the single most damaging property for loop stability because the controller acts on stale information.

questions.question: The process time constant is:

options.A: The total time to reach the new steady state
options.B: The time to reach about 63 percent of the total change after the response begins
options.C: The dead time plus the settling time

questions.rationale: One time constant is 63.2 percent of the final change. Roughly five time constants gives effective completion.

questions.question: A loop with a high ratio of dead time to time constant is:

options.B: Difficult to control and requires detuning

questions.rationale: Dead time forces you to reduce gain, because the controller is always responding to a past state. This is why long transport lags are designed out where possible.

questions.question: A self-regulating process is one that:

options.B: Settles at a new steady state after a step change in output

questions.rationale: Self-regulating processes find a new equilibrium. Flow and temperature usually do; level in a tank does not.

questions.question: Why must controller action be considered separately from controller tuning?

options.A: Tuning is done by the vendor
options.B: Wrong action makes the loop unstable at any tuning; wrong tuning only makes it perform badly
options.C: Action affects only the alarm limits

questions.rationale: Action is a yes/no correctness question. Tuning is an optimisation. No amount of tuning fixes wrong action.

questions.question: In a loop with a reverse-acting controller, increasing the setpoint will:

options.B: Increase the controller output

questions.rationale: Raising the setpoint increases the error SP minus PV, and a reverse-acting controller increases output for increasing error. This is the point people most often get backwards.

questions.question: The overall loop gain is approximately:

options.B: The product of controller gain, valve gain, process gain and transmitter gain
options.C: The sum of the individual gains
options.D: The process gain divided by the controller gain

questions.rationale: Gains multiply around the loop. This is why changing a transmitter range or a valve trim detunes a loop that was previously stable.

questions.question: A transmitter range is narrowed from 0-200 degC to 0-100 degC without retuning. The effect on loop gain is:

options.B: Doubled

questions.rationale: The same temperature change now produces twice the percentage signal, so loop gain doubles and the loop may become unstable. Range changes require retuning.

questions.question: An equal-percentage valve characteristic is often chosen because:

options.B: Its gain varies in a way that compensates for falling process gain at high flow

questions.rationale: The valve's rising gain offsets the process's falling gain, giving a more constant loop gain across the range. Installed characteristic, not inherent, is what matters.

questions.question: A loop is stable at low load and oscillates at high load. The most likely cause is:

options.B: Loop gain varying with operating point because of valve or process non-linearity

questions.rationale: Non-linearity moves the loop gain with operating point. Tuning for one end of the range then destabilises the other.

questions.question: Why is a step test performed with the controller in manual?

options.B: So the observed response is the process alone, uncontaminated by controller action
options.E: To satisfy the permit to work

questions.rationale: In auto the controller is also acting, so you cannot separate the process response from the controller's. Manual isolates the process.

questions.question: The term open-loop response refers to:

options.A: Response with the loop in auto
options.B: Response with the controller in manual, so no feedback path is active

questions.rationale: Open loop means the feedback path is broken - controller in manual. This is the condition under which the reaction curve test is done.

questions.question: A reverse-acting controller's output INCREASES when its setpoint increases. Why does this matter in a cascade?

options.A: It does not matter in cascade
options.B: The outer controller's output is the inner setpoint, so the sign convention must be traced through both loops
options.C: It changes the inner loop's fail action
options.D: It affects only the alarm limits
options.E: It requires derivative on both loops

questions.rationale: In cascade the outer output is the inner setpoint, so you must trace the sign through both controllers and the valve. Getting one wrong makes the pair unstable even though each looks correct alone.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: In a temperature-to-flow cascade on a heat exchanger, the outer temperature controller's output is:

options.B: The setpoint of the inner flow controller

questions.rationale: Outer output becomes inner setpoint. The inner flow controller then positions the valve.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: In that cascade, which controller must be tuned first?

options.B: The inner flow controller
options.E: The one with the longer time constant

questions.rationale: Tune the inner loop first and leave it in auto, then tune the outer against it. Tuning the outer first means retuning everything when the inner changes.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: A loop's PV cycles continuously with a regular period even though the process is steady. The most likely cause is:

options.B: Controller gain too high or integral too fast

questions.rationale: Regular sustained cycling is the signature of over-aggressive tuning. Wrong action drives to a limit rather than cycling.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: A loop's output shows a sawtooth pattern while the PV shows a square wave. This pattern indicates:

options.B: Valve stiction

questions.rationale: Sawtooth OP with square PV is the classic stick-slip signature. No amount of retuning fixes a sticking valve - the valve must be repaired.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: A loop is slow to return to setpoint after a disturbance but never overshoots. The likely tuning fault is:

options.B: Gain too low or integral too slow

questions.rationale: Sluggish and non-oscillatory means the controller is too weak. Increase gain or shorten integral time.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: A loop overshoots badly on a setpoint change but rejects load disturbances well. The best first remedy is:

options.B: Apply setpoint ramping or use a controller structure that acts derivative and proportional on PV rather than error

questions.rationale: The problem is only on setpoint changes, so change how the setpoint enters the controller rather than detuning disturbance rejection that already works.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: In an override arrangement, a low selector passes:

options.A: The higher of two controller outputs
options.B: The lower of two controller outputs
options.E: The output of the loop in auto

questions.rationale: A low selector passes the lower output, which in a fail-closed arrangement means the more conservative demand wins.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: In an override scheme, what must be done to the controller that is NOT currently selected?

options.B: Prevent its integral term from winding up

questions.rationale: The deselected controller's integral will wind up while its output goes nowhere, so it takes over badly when selected. External reset or integral tracking prevents this.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: Select all things you would check before concluding that a loop simply needs retuning.

options.B: Valve is stroking freely and the positioner is calibrated
options.C: Transmitter is in calibration and the range is correct
options.D: The process is at its normal operating point

questions.rationale: Action, valve, measurement and operating point. Retuning a loop with a sticking valve or a wrong range wastes a day and fixes nothing.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: A controller is in auto, the error is large, and the output sits at 100 percent without moving. This indicates:

options.B: The output is saturated and the loop cannot meet the demand

questions.rationale: Saturation. The controller is asking for everything it has and it is not enough - which is a process or equipment capacity problem, not a tuning one.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: An operator reports that a loop 'fights itself' with another loop nearby. This is:

options.B: Loop interaction, where two loops manipulate variables that affect each other
options.E: A sign of wrong controller action

questions.rationale: Interaction is real and common - drum level and drum pressure, or two loops on a shared header. The remedy is detuning one, decoupling, or a multivariable strategy.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: When a loop is switched from manual to auto and the output jumps immediately, the likely cause is:

options.B: Bumpless transfer is not configured or the integral has not been initialised to the current output

questions.rationale: On transfer the integral must be preloaded to the current output. If it is not, the output jumps to whatever the algorithm computes from scratch.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: A feedforward signal is added to a temperature loop. Its purpose is to:

options.B: Act on a measured disturbance before it affects the PV

questions.rationale: Feedforward acts on a disturbance before the PV moves. It is almost always combined with feedback trim, because no model is perfect.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: On a ratio control scheme, the wild stream is:

options.B: The stream you measure but do not control, which the other is ratioed to
options.C: The stream with the highest flow
options.D: The stream with the widest range

questions.rationale: The wild stream is uncontrolled and measured; the captive stream is manipulated to hold the ratio to it.
questions.moduleTopic: Analysing controller action in a strategy

questions.question: In a Ziegler-Nichols open-loop (reaction curve) test, the three parameters extracted from the response are:

options.B: Process gain, dead time and time constant
options.C: Ultimate gain, ultimate period and damping
options.D: Rise time, settling time and peak time

questions.rationale: Process gain Kp, dead time, and time constant. Every open-loop tuning rule is a formula in those three numbers.

questions.question: Why is the open-loop step method preferred over the closed-loop ultimate gain method on an operating plant?

options.B: It does not require driving the loop into sustained oscillation
options.C: It works on integrating processes only
options.E: It can be done in auto

questions.rationale: The closed-loop method requires deliberately destabilising the loop until it oscillates. On a running plant that is often unacceptable and sometimes unsafe.

questions.question: How large should the step change in controller output be for a reaction curve test?

options.A: As small as possible, under 0.1 percent
options.B: Large enough to produce a clear response well above the noise, but small enough not to upset the plant
options.D: Whatever moves the valve to its stop

questions.rationale: Big enough to see clearly above noise, small enough to be tolerable. Typically 5 to 10 percent, and it should be done in both directions to expose hysteresis.

questions.question: Why should a step test be repeated in the opposite direction?

options.A: To confirm the transmitter is linear
options.B: To reveal valve hysteresis, stiction or an asymmetric process gain
options.D: To satisfy the permit to work

questions.rationale: A different response up versus down exposes stiction or non-linearity. Tuning from one direction only can produce settings that are wrong for half the operating range.

questions.question: A reaction curve test gives dead time 2 minutes, time constant 10 minutes and process gain 2.0. Using the Ziegler-Nichols open-loop PI rule Kc = 0.9 x tau / (Kp x theta), what is the controller gain? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: 0.9 x 10 divided by (2.0 x 2) equals 2.25. Note the gain falls as dead time rises - which is the mathematical statement of why dead time forces detuning.

questions.question: For the same test (dead time 2 minutes), the Ziegler-Nichols open-loop PI rule sets integral time Ti = 3.33 x theta. What is Ti in minutes? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: 3.33 x 2 equals 6.66 minutes. Integral time scales with dead time, not with the time constant.

questions.question: Using the Ziegler-Nichols open-loop PID rule Kc = 1.2 x tau / (Kp x theta), with tau 12 minutes, theta 3 minutes and Kp 1.5, what is the controller gain? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: 1.2 x 12 divided by (1.5 x 3) equals 3.2.

questions.question: In the reaction curve method, the time constant is measured from:

options.A: The moment the step is applied
options.B: The moment the PV first begins to move, to 63 percent of its total change
options.C: The moment the PV reaches setpoint
options.D: The start of the test to the end of the test
options.E: Peak to peak of the oscillation

questions.rationale: Time constant is measured from the start of the response - after the dead time has elapsed - to 63.2 percent of the total change.

questions.question: Select all conditions that must hold for a valid reaction curve test.

options.B: The process is at a steady operating point before the step
options.C: No other disturbance occurs during the test
options.D: The loop is in cascade with its outer loop in auto
options.E: The response is allowed to reach a new steady state

questions.rationale: Manual, steady before, undisturbed during, and allowed to settle. If the outer cascade loop is in auto it will fight the test.

questions.question: A step test on a level loop shows the level rising steadily and never settling. This means:

options.B: The process is integrating, so the reaction curve method must be adapted

questions.rationale: Integrating processes never settle, so self-regulating tuning rules do not apply directly. Use an integrating-process rule or lambda tuning instead.

questions.question: Ziegler-Nichols settings were designed to give:

options.B: Quarter-amplitude damping, roughly a 25 percent decay ratio
options.D: Fastest possible response with no oscillation

questions.rationale: Quarter-amplitude damping - a deliberately oscillatory design criterion. It is far too aggressive for most process loops, which is why ZN settings are usually a starting point, not a final answer.

questions.question: Having calculated Ziegler-Nichols settings, common practice is to:

options.A: Apply them exactly and lock the loop
options.B: Apply roughly half the calculated gain as a starting point and observe
options.C: Double the gain for faster response

questions.rationale: Halving the ZN gain is a widely used practical correction, because the original criterion accepts more oscillation than a process plant should.

questions.question: The Cohen-Coon method is generally preferred over Ziegler-Nichols when:

options.B: Dead time is significant relative to the time constant

questions.rationale: Cohen-Coon was developed for dead-time dominant processes, typically where dead time over time constant exceeds about 0.3.

questions.question: Lambda tuning differs from Ziegler-Nichols in that the engineer specifies:

options.B: The desired closed-loop time constant

questions.rationale: In lambda tuning you choose the closed-loop speed you want and the settings follow. That makes the result predictable and repeatable.

questions.question: Why is lambda tuning often chosen for loops that interact with each other?

options.B: It produces a non-oscillatory response and lets you deliberately separate the speeds of interacting loops
options.C: It removes the need for integral action
options.D: It compensates for dead time automatically

questions.rationale: Because you set the closed-loop speed, you can make one loop deliberately slower than another so they stop fighting. Aggressive tuning on both is what creates interaction problems.

questions.question: A larger lambda value produces a loop that is:

options.B: Slower and more robust

questions.rationale: Lambda is the target closed-loop time constant, so a bigger lambda means slower and more tolerant of model error.

questions.question: In the Ziegler-Nichols closed-loop method, the ultimate gain Ku is:

options.A: The maximum gain the controller can be set to
options.B: The proportional gain at which the loop oscillates with constant amplitude, with I and D off
options.D: The gain at which the valve saturates

questions.rationale: Ku is the P-only gain producing sustained constant-amplitude oscillation. Pu is the period of that oscillation.

questions.question: A closed-loop test gives an ultimate gain of 4.0 and an ultimate period of 8 minutes. Using the Ziegler-Nichols PID rule Kc = 0.6 x Ku, what controller gain results? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: 0.6 x 4.0 equals 2.4.

questions.question: For the same test (Pu = 8 minutes), the Ziegler-Nichols PID rules give Ti = 0.5 x Pu. What is the integral time in minutes? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: 0.5 x 8 equals 4 minutes. The derivative time would be 0.125 x Pu, or 1 minute.

questions.question: For the same test (Pu = 8 minutes), the Ziegler-Nichols PID rule gives Td = 0.125 x Pu. What is the derivative time in minutes? Enter a number.
questions.rationale: 0.125 x 8 equals 1 minute. Note Ti is always four times Td in the classic ZN PID rule.

questions.question: Select all valid criticisms of applying Ziegler-Nichols settings unmodified on a process plant.

options.A: The design criterion accepts about 25 percent overshoot
options.B: The closed-loop test requires deliberately destabilising the loop
options.C: It does not suit integrating processes well
options.D: It cannot be calculated without a historian
options.E: It assumes a first-order plus dead time model that not all processes match

questions.rationale: All except the historian point - a trend recorder or even a chart is enough. The real objections are the oscillatory design target and the model assumption.

questions.question: A loop must reject disturbances quickly but setpoint changes are rare. Tuning should prioritise:

options.B: Disturbance rejection, accepting some setpoint overshoot

questions.rationale: Tune for the job the loop actually does. Most process loops sit at a fixed setpoint and spend their lives rejecting disturbances.

questions.question: Which tuning approach is most appropriate for a surge tank level loop feeding a downstream unit?

options.A: Tight lambda tuning for fast level control
options.B: Averaging level control, deliberately slow, letting the level swing within limits
options.E: P-only with a very narrow proportional band

questions.rationale: Averaging level control. The vessel exists to absorb variation, so the level should be allowed to move and the outflow kept steady.

questions.question: After retuning a loop, what should be recorded?

options.B: Old settings, new settings, the test data, the date and the reason for the change
options.E: The valve position at the time

questions.rationale: Old and new settings with the test data and reason. Without the old values you cannot revert, and without the reason nobody knows in two years whether it is still valid.

questions.question: The essential requirement for a cascade to work is that the inner loop must be:

options.B: Significantly faster than the outer loop
options.C: The same speed as the outer loop

questions.rationale: The inner loop must be fast enough to settle before the outer loop reacts - commonly a factor of three to five in speed. Otherwise the two fight.

questions.question: The main benefit of cascade control is that it:

options.B: Rejects disturbances in the inner variable before they reach the primary variable
options.E: Removes the need for integral action

questions.rationale: The inner loop catches its own disturbances early. A supply pressure change is corrected by the flow loop before the temperature ever moves.

questions.question: In a temperature-to-flow cascade, which is the primary (master) loop?

options.B: The temperature loop
options.D: The one with the higher gain

questions.rationale: The primary is the variable you actually care about - temperature. The flow loop is the secondary that does its bidding.

questions.question: Which controller in a cascade normally has integral action, and why?

options.A: Only the inner, to remove offset quickly
options.B: Both, but the outer must have it because it is the loop that must sit exactly on setpoint
options.C: Only the outer, because the inner cannot

questions.rationale: The primary must reach its setpoint exactly, so it needs integral. The secondary often has it too, but a small offset there is corrected by the primary anyway.

questions.question: If the inner loop of a cascade is switched to manual, what happens to the outer loop?

options.B: It loses its final control path and will wind up
options.C: It automatically switches to direct action
options.D: It takes over the valve directly

questions.rationale: The outer loop's output no longer reaches anything, so its integral winds up. Proper cascade implementations track the inner setpoint back to the outer output to prevent this.

questions.question: Select all conditions that must be satisfied for cascade control to be worthwhile.

options.B: The inner loop responds significantly faster than the outer
options.C: Significant disturbances enter through the inner variable
options.E: The inner variable is influenced by the same final control element
